features.meta.description.message: Everything CloudGround does on your Ubuntu server: speed, sites and apps, deploys, data, security, visibility and access, each linked to its guide.

features.bench.uncached.message: No cache: PHP and the database

features.bench.caption.message: Requests per second, mean of three runs

features.bench.note.message: 2 vCPU VPS, Ubuntu 26.04, a WooCommerce shop, release v0.1.0.

features.flow.staging.message: the copy where you try your changes

features.flow.snapshot.message: of production, verified before anything changes

features.record.restoreText.message: one file, one database or the whole site

features.cli.caption.message: The same moves, from a terminal

features.speed.intro.message: Every site has its own page cache, on a server tuned to the machine. The figures are measured on a 2 vCPU VPS.

features.speed.cache.text.message: nginx serves pages from the cache without waking PHP, compresses them once and keeps serving them while they refresh.

features.speed.purge.text.message: Change a post or a price and the WordPress connector purges only the pages that show it. One URL or the whole site, when you need to.

features.speed.tuning.text.message: PHP, OPcache and MariaDB are sized from the server’s memory and CPU count, with PHP’s JIT switched on.

features.speed.devmode.text.message: While you work, the page cache steps aside for 15, 30 or 60 minutes, then switches itself back on.

features.speed.resources.text.message: CPU, memory, tasks and disk for every site, with 24-hour and 30-day history, and limits that apply without a restart.

features.sites.intro.message: Besides WordPress, you can run PHP, Laravel, static sites, reverse proxies and Node.js or Python apps. Each has its own user and sandbox.

features.sites.types.text.message: WordPress, WooCommerce, PHP, Laravel, static and reverse proxy, each with its own Unix user, PHP-FPM master and systemd sandbox.

features.sites.wizard.text.message: A wizard creates the site, checks that the domain’s DNS points at the server and hands you a summary to keep.

features.sites.apps.text.message: Node.js 20, 22 or 24, checked against its published checksums, or the server’s Python in a virtual environment per site. The app runs as a service of the site’s own user, behind nginx.

features.sites.functions.text.message: Node.js or Python code in several files, with its own dependencies, that belongs to no site. A shared address or one of its own, an optional token and CORS, a system user per function. It runs only when it’s called or scheduled.

features.sites.wpupdates.text.message: From the buttons or on a schedule, behind a tested snapshot. The site is measured before and after, and restored on its own if the update breaks it.

features.sites.domains.text.message: Aliases, plus Let’s Encrypt certificates, wildcards included, or your own.

features.sites.redirects.text.message: One canonical name, with or without www, and up to 200 exact or prefix 301/302 redirects. They’re answered before the page cache.

features.sites.mail.text.message: mail() and wp_mail go out through an SMTP relay, server-wide or per site, with a test send and an SPF, DKIM and DMARC checklist.

features.sites.maintenance.text.message: Visitors get a 503 with your title and message, while listed addresses and a preview link still see the site.

features.deploys.intro.message: Code lives in releases. A new one goes live only once it’s ready, and the previous one is always a step away.

features.deploys.releases.text.message: Every deploy builds a release of its own and puts it live. Apps install their dependencies per release, and a failed install leaves the live one live.

features.deploys.staging.text.message: A copy of the site to try your changes on. It sends no email.

features.deploys.safepush.text.message: Promotes your changes only when Performance Guard’s measurements hold up, after taking a safety snapshot of production.

features.deploys.git.text.message: A per-site webhook for GitHub, GitLab, Gitea and Forgejo builds a release from a branch on every push. For private repositories, the panel makes a deploy key.

features.deploys.rollback.text.message: Go back to an earlier release. For Node.js and Python apps, exactly what that release installed comes back with it.

features.data.intro.message: Every backup is restored as a test. You can take back just the part you need.

features.data.backups.text.message: Encrypted with restic at the hour you pick, then restored as a test.

features.data.destinations.text.message: S3-compatible storage, Backblaze B2, SFTP or a folder on the server. For SFTP, the panel makes the key.

features.data.restore.text.message: The whole site, only the files, some of its databases, or a single file or folder, always behind a tested safety snapshot.

features.data.download.text.message: Streamed as an archive, for administrators and for operators on their own sites. Every download lands in the audit log.

features.data.external.text.message: Register a MariaDB/MySQL or PostgreSQL server and create a site’s databases there. Backups, restores and exports follow them.

features.data.quarry.text.message: The database tool at /quarry: browse, edit, search, import and export. Simulate runs a write inside a transaction that is always rolled back.

features.data.move.title.message: Move a site from another host

features.data.move.text.message: Give the old server’s SSH or SFTP access and look at a dry run first. CloudGround then copies the files and the database behind a safety snapshot, and keeps the password nowhere.

features.data.cleanup.text.message: Weekly, if you turn it on: expired transients go, and each post keeps its last N revisions.

features.security.intro.message: A compromised site can’t see its neighbours, password guessers get blocked at the firewall, and known holes get flagged.

features.security.isolation.text.message: Its own system user, PHP-FPM and systemd sandbox, with a private /dev/shm and IPC namespace. A compromised site can’t see the others.

features.security.firewall.text.message: The panel shows you the rules before it turns the firewall on, and keeps the real SSH port, the web ports and its own port open.

features.security.blocklist.text.message: Addresses that keep failing to sign in to the panel, SSH, wp-login or xmlrpc are blocked at the firewall for a while. Addresses on the allowlist never are.

features.security.refuse.text.message: Turn a site’s visitors away by address or network, user agent or country.

features.security.hardening.text.message: One-click hardening, each item separate and reversible, plus two-factor sign-in for WordPress accounts.

features.security.vulns.text.message: WordPress core, plugins and themes are checked against a public database. You see which versions have known issues and which version fixes them.

features.security.malware.text.message: Turn it on and ClamAV checks a site’s files on a schedule or on demand, quarantines what it flags and raises an alert.

features.security.passkeys.text.message: Sign in with a fingerprint, your face or a PIN. Ten single-use codes for the day you lose your phone, and two-step verification required if you say so.

features.security.roles.text.message: Administrator, operator on the sites you assign, read-only.

features.security.audit.text.message: Changes are recorded in the audit log, along with every log and backup download.

features.security.protect.text.message: Put a username and password in front of any path on a site.

features.security.ubuntu.text.message: Pending packages, security ones first, installed all at once or security only. Plus a notice when the server needs a reboot.

features.visibility.intro.message: Traffic, logs and site health stay on your server. If something breaks, the panel alerts you.

features.visibility.traffic.text.message: Requests, page views, visitors, bots, status codes and cache hits, read from the site’s own logs on the server. No cookies, and no addresses stored.

features.visibility.logs.text.message: Server and site logs in the panel. Download a site’s full logs, rotated ones included, from the panel or with cgctl logs.

features.visibility.uptime.text.message: Switch it on and the server checks the site every minute, then alerts you after two failures in a row.

features.visibility.alerts.text.message: Sites over their limits, sites that stop answering, suspicious files: the alert reaches you by email or webhook, with every operation named in plain words.

features.visibility.cloudflare.text.message: The panel sees the visitor’s real address, the block list still applies, and a purge from the panel clears Cloudflare’s cache too.

features.access.intro.message: Everything in the panel also works from a terminal or over the API. An AI assistant can do it only after you switch it on.

features.access.cgctl.text.message: The panel’s command line: sites, backups, releases, logs, blocking and more, on the server or from another machine.

features.access.tokens.text.message: One token per script. Revoke it when you no longer need it.

features.access.api.text.message: The HTTP API that cgctl talks to, documented for anyone writing their own tools.

features.access.mcp.text.message: Off until you turn it on. Then Claude, ChatGPT and other MCP clients can manage the server over OAuth: you approve each connection with your password and a second factor, and destructive actions wait for you to confirm them in the panel.

features.access.sftp.text.message: SFTP accounts per site, keys only if you like, and a shell that runs as the site’s own user.

features.access.update.text.message: Signed releases, from the panel or with cgctl update. If the new release doesn’t come up, the panel rolls itself back.

features.hero.lede.message: One control panel for one Ubuntu server, in seven areas. Each feature gets two lines and a link to its guide.

features.hero.demoNote.message: The demo runs in your browser on sample data. Nothing leaves the page.

features.closing.text.message: The demo is the real panel with sample data. Installing it takes one command.

home.features.speed.text.message: nginx serves pages without waking PHP and purges only the ones that change. PHP, OPcache and MariaDB are tuned to the machine.

home.features.sites.text.message: WordPress, WooCommerce, PHP, Laravel, static sites, proxies and Node.js and Python apps, plus standalone functions with an address of their own. Each under its own user, in its own sandbox.

home.features.deploys.text.message: Staging, Safe Push that holds back a slower release, deploys from Git on every push, and the previous release always one step away.

home.features.data.text.message: Encrypted backups to S3, B2, SFTP or a local folder, each one restored as a test. Take back one file, one database or the whole site.

home.features.security.text2.message: Per-site isolation, a firewall and block lists, vulnerability and malware scans, passkeys, roles and an audit log.

home.features.visibility.text.message: Statistics from the server’s own logs, uptime checks, alerts by email or webhook, logs you can download.

home.features.access.title.message: cgctl, the API and AI assistants

home.features.access.text.message: Everything works from a terminal or over the API too. An MCP server for AI assistants stays off until you turn it on.

home.features.intro2.message: What you would normally set up by hand is on from your first site. Seven areas.

home.features.all.text.message: Each one in two lines, with a link to its guide.
